pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for where the first bass entrance feels strongest. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Where would half a beat of silence make the drop hit harder?

Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.

Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the first bass attack, then restore it after the kick. The attack should land harder when it has room.

tracks.skill: You should hear the reply without a gain jump.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the first answer moves pitch or timbre. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Try following the vocal rhythm first, then count where you would leave a gap for it.
tracks.bass: Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then make bar two an audible answer to bar one. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for whether the first answer moves pitch or timbre. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Try following the vocal rhythm first, then count where you would leave a gap for it.

Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.

Loop two bars, then make bar two an audible answer to bar one. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: change only the filter peak on the second bass sound. You should hear the reply without a gain jump.

record.label: Digital Soundboy
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Count back two beats from an entrance and decide where a short bass pickup would fit.
tracks.bass: Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Try tapping a short response in a space between the vocal phrases.

Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.

Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

record.label: Charge Recordings
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Count which accents you would repeat and which one you would replace with a fill.
tracks.bass: Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop. Count which accents you would repeat and which one you would replace with a fill.

Drive a short saw into Saturator for an audible mid layer. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Anchor the snare on beats two and four. Put a quiet pickup just before the second snare and keep kick transients clear of the sub.

Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with Operator on a sine carrier and a sine modulator 2 octaves up. Keep the brighter FM decay around 34 ms. High-pass that sound near 120 Hz after Saturator and let a second centred sine supply the weight.
tracks.groove: Put a kick on each quarter note and the bass in the intervening gaps. Let the clap stay straight and test a quiet pickup into bar two.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with Operator on a sine carrier and a sine modulator 2 octaves up. Keep the brighter FM decay around 34 ms. High-pass that sound near 120 Hz after Saturator and let a second centred sine supply the weight.

Put a kick on each quarter note and the bass in the intervening gaps. Let the clap stay straight and test a quiet pickup into bar two.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

record.label: Bounce Paradise
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with Operator on a sine carrier and a sine modulator 2 octaves up. Keep the brighter FM decay around 44 ms. High-pass that sound near 120 Hz after Saturator and let a second centred sine supply the weight.
tracks.groove: Put a kick on each quarter note and the bass in the intervening gaps. Let the clap stay straight and test a quiet pickup into bar two.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with Operator on a sine carrier and a sine modulator 2 octaves up. Keep the brighter FM decay around 44 ms. High-pass that sound near 120 Hz after Saturator and let a second centred sine supply the weight.

Put a kick on each quarter note and the bass in the intervening gaps. Let the clap stay straight and test a quiet pickup into bar two.

Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how quieter percussion pushes the pattern forward. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.

Loop two bars, then introduce the ghost hit only in the second phrase. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

tracks.skill: Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

tracks.skill: The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

record.label: Cyclops Recordings
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for which cue makes the pattern want to repeat. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: remove the final two steps, then compare with the full loop. Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for which cue makes the pattern want to repeat. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Keep a dry sine beneath a driven square-wave answer. Separate the movement and the weight on two tracks. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Place the snare on beat three. Let the second kick land in a gap, then try a short bass reply that ends before the next snare.

Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: remove the final two steps, then compare with the full loop. Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.

record.label: Nano Records
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how quieter percussion pushes the pattern forward. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.
tracks.groove: Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then introduce the ghost hit only in the second phrase. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the ghost hit and bring it back at velocity 38. The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.

record.label: KANTARA
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.
tracks.groove: Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.

Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.

Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

tracks.title: Oxidation (Original mix)

record.label: Iboga Records
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for what a tail can add after a phrase ends. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.
tracks.groove: Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then close the send before the next downbeat. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: automate the delay send on the last bright note only. The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for what a tail can add after a phrase ends. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.

Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.

Loop two bars, then close the send before the next downbeat. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: automate the delay send on the last bright note only. The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.

record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The attack should land harder when it has room.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for where the first bass entrance feels strongest. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.
tracks.groove: Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the first bass attack, then restore it after the kick. The attack should land harder when it has room.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for where the first bass entrance feels strongest. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.

Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.

Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the first bass attack, then restore it after the kick. The attack should land harder when it has room.

record.label: Armind (Armada)
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.
tracks.groove: Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Start with a mono Drift saw with a quick filter decay and 12 ms amp release. Set Auto Filter near 1.2 kHz. Let that pluck carry the rhythm, and bring in a very quiet centred sine only where the note needs weight.

Keep a short four-on-the-floor kick and put three straight bass hits between each pair. Compare two clean downbeats before adding shaker accents.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

record.label: Cleveland City
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.

Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

tracks.title: Fear

record.label: NOIX Records
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.

Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

tracks.title: Ghost

record.label: Banana Club
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Keep the movement audible when the loop goes mono.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the bass still reads when the sounds get wide. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then widen only the lead on the reply. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: compare the loop with Utility at 0% and 100% Width. Keep the movement audible when the loop goes mono.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for whether the bass still reads when the sounds get wide. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.

Loop two bars, then widen only the lead on the reply. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: compare the loop with Utility at 0% and 100% Width. Keep the movement audible when the loop goes mono.

record.label: Primitive UK
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The attack should land harder when it has room.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for where the first bass entrance feels strongest. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the first bass attack, then restore it after the kick. The attack should land harder when it has room.

pages.text:

Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.

Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

tracks.title: Freedom 2

record.label: Kwengface LTD
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try a short, high-passed synth chop to reply to a sliced break while a dry sine holds the lower pitch. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a fixed snare and an original broken kick. Move only one quiet slice in the second bar to hear how a fill swings against the beat.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

record.label: Tasty Recordings
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try the low register as a repeated riff and use a brighter octave reply. Shorten that reply so it leaves room for the next root note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Keep clap on two and four. Make the hat before the clap slightly softer and let the higher bass octave hit on a different part of the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

record.label: Tasty Recordings

tracks.skill: You should hear the reply without a gain jump.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for whether the first answer moves pitch or timbre. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try the low register as a repeated riff and use a brighter octave reply. Shorten that reply so it leaves room for the next root note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Keep clap on two and four. Make the hat before the clap slightly softer and let the higher bass octave hit on a different part of the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then make bar two an audible answer to bar one. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: change only the filter peak on the second bass sound. You should hear the reply without a gain jump.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for whether the first answer moves pitch or timbre. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try the low register as a repeated riff and use a brighter octave reply. Shorten that reply so it leaves room for the next root note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Keep clap on two and four. Make the hat before the clap slightly softer and let the higher bass octave hit on a different part of the beat.

Loop two bars, then make bar two an audible answer to bar one. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: change only the filter peak on the second bass sound. You should hear the reply without a gain jump.

tracks.skill: The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how quieter percussion pushes the pattern forward. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Try the low register as a repeated riff and use a brighter octave reply. Shorten that reply so it leaves room for the next root note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Keep clap on two and four. Make the hat before the clap slightly softer and let the higher bass octave hit on a different part of the beat.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then introduce the ghost hit only in the second phrase. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the ghost hit and bring it back at velocity 38. The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how quieter percussion pushes the pattern forward. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Try the low register as a repeated riff and use a brighter octave reply. Shorten that reply so it leaves room for the next root note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Keep clap on two and four. Make the hat before the clap slightly softer and let the higher bass octave hit on a different part of the beat.

Loop two bars, then introduce the ghost hit only in the second phrase. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the ghost hit and bring it back at velocity 38. The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.

tracks.title: Get Loose (Extended Mix)

record.label: Dansu Discs
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.

Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

tracks.skill: Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for which cue makes the pattern want to repeat. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: remove the final two steps, then compare with the full loop. Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.

pages.text:

Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.

Loop two bars, then make bar two an audible answer to bar one. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.

record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

record.label: Rinse
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Keep a warm sine underneath a quieter filtered tone. Try moving the cutoff slowly over the repeated note. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Start with a short kick on each quarter. Lower the second hat of each bar and use a small amount of swing on hats and bass while the clap anchors the groove.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

tracks.skill: The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for what a tail can add after a phrase ends. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then close the send before the next downbeat. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Check the level with Utility before choosing a version. Turn it down to see if the bass pulse still reads against the kick.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: automate the delay send on the last bright note only. The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.

tracks.bass: Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: remove the final two steps, then compare with the full loop. Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for which cue makes the pattern want to repeat. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.

Loop two bars, then end one repetition in silence before the next entrance. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: remove the final two steps, then compare with the full loop. Choose the version whose return feels most deliberate.

record.label: Virgin
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.

Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

tracks.skill: The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.
tracks.groove: Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how a sound decays into the next accent. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Use a clipped, filtered square sound and leave room for the percussion answers. For the stock Live exercise, use Operator or Drift, then Saturator at +2 dB and EQ Eight high-passed at 120 Hz on the upper track only. Keep the low sine dry and centre it.

Use a steady kick and two percussion timbres that trade spaces. Move one quiet rim hit before the next kick and listen for the resulting pickup.

Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Drop a kick into Simpler on a separate channel and start playback just after the transient. High-pass the rumble around 35 Hz and low-pass it near 180 Hz with EQ Eight. Use separate faders for the kick and tail so the attack stays readable.
tracks.groove: Use a solid quarter-note kick with short offbeat hats. Set the rumble just below the kick and mute the hats to check that the low rhythm stays clear.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

tracks.skill: The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for when a hook would interfere with the centre of the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Drop a kick into Simpler on a separate channel and start playback just after the transient. High-pass the rumble around 35 Hz and low-pass it near 180 Hz with EQ Eight. Use separate faders for the kick and tail so the attack stays readable.
tracks.groove: Use a solid quarter-note kick with short offbeat hats. Set the rumble just below the kick and mute the hats to check that the low rhythm stays clear.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then save the higher response for the next repetition. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Keep the bass dry in the centre. High-pass Return A so reverb adds depth without masking the low-middle notes.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: move a response up one octave on the mid track. The upper reply should remain audible at the same low-end level.

On the recording, listen for whether the sound moves within the note. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Drop a kick into Simpler on a separate channel and start playback just after the transient. High-pass the rumble around 35 Hz and low-pass it near 180 Hz with EQ Eight. Use separate faders for the kick and tail so the attack stays readable.

Use a solid quarter-note kick with short offbeat hats. Set the rumble just below the kick and mute the hats to check that the low rhythm stays clear.

Loop two bars, then open the filter further on one response only. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Recheck in mono after adding saturation. If the low end becomes harder to hear, keep Utility Width low on the bass alone.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: halve the opening envelope decay and level-match the two versions. Keep the movement that reads clearly without harshness.

pages.text:

Drop a kick into Simpler on a separate channel and start playback just after the transient. High-pass the rumble around 35 Hz and low-pass it near 180 Hz with EQ Eight. Use separate faders for the kick and tail so the attack stays readable.

Use a solid quarter-note kick with short offbeat hats. Set the rumble just below the kick and mute the hats to check that the low rhythm stays clear.

Loop two bars, then mute the final low note once per four bars. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: reduce the amp release by half and listen across the kicks. The next drum hit should land firmly without a click.

tracks.skill: The attack should land harder when it has room.

tracks.bass: Use Operator with a sine and a falling pitch envelope from +12 semitones to zero over about 62 ms. Try a separate dry sine only under the sustained notes. High-pass the shaker and click layer when it overlaps the low tone.

tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a short gap before the next low accent. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

record.label: Piano Hub
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Use Operator with a sine and a falling pitch envelope from +12 semitones to zero over about 62 ms. Try a separate dry sine only under the sustained notes. High-pass the shaker and click layer when it overlaps the low tone.
tracks.groove: Keep a soft four-to-the-floor kick and leave space for two shakers with different accents. Change the second log-drum answer while the kick stays fixed.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for how much space the kick has under the bass. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Use Operator with a sine and a falling pitch envelope from +12 semitones to zero over about 62 ms. Try a separate dry sine only under the sustained notes. High-pass the shaker and click layer when it overlaps the low tone.

Keep a soft four-to-the-floor kick and leave space for two shakers with different accents. Change the second log-drum answer while the kick stays fixed.

Loop two bars, then leave a hole at the end of the phrase for a kick fill. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: shorten the longest bass note by one sixteenth. Listen for a clearer kick without losing the bass movement.

Loop two bars, then introduce the ghost hit only in the second phrase. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Match the apparent loudness. A brighter sound will seem bigger even if it obscures the percussion.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: mute the ghost hit and bring it back at velocity 38. The main snare should remain the strongest rhythmic cue.

record.label: Lea Records
record.context: Recording key, tempo and swing unverified. Workshop settings refer to the original exercises.

tracks.skill: The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.
tracks.listen: On the recording, listen for what a tail can add after a phrase ends. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.
tracks.bass: Use Operator with a sine and a falling pitch envelope from +12 semitones to zero over about 62 ms. Try a separate dry sine only under the sustained notes. High-pass the shaker and click layer when it overlaps the low tone.
tracks.groove: Keep a soft four-to-the-floor kick and leave space for two shakers with different accents. Change the second log-drum answer while the kick stays fixed.
tracks.arrangement: Loop two bars, then close the send before the next downbeat. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.
tracks.mix: Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.
tracks.exercise: Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: automate the delay send on the last bright note only. The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.

pages.label: Song guide
pages.text:
On the recording, listen for what a tail can add after a phrase ends. Mark the place you want to compare with the original practice loop.

Use Operator with a sine and a falling pitch envelope from +12 semitones to zero over about 62 ms. Try a separate dry sine only under the sustained notes. High-pass the shaker and click layer when it overlaps the low tone.

Keep a soft four-to-the-floor kick and leave space for two shakers with different accents. Change the second log-drum answer while the kick stays fixed.

Loop two bars, then close the send before the next downbeat. Keep one rhythmic detail the same so you can hear what the change does.

Filter the repeats after Delay B. Taking low end out of the repeats leaves the next dry hit easier to hear.

Spend eight minutes on a duplicate of the clip. Try this: automate the delay send on the last bright note only. The echo should fit in the gap and leave the dry note clear.
